entries.title: The Transversal Invariant
entries.body:
I got the question wrong the first time.  The SAT asked: "A transversal cuts two parallel lines … which of these sums could **not** equal four of the angles?"  The textbook expects you to list all five cases, but I was lazy and started looking for a way out.

What fell out of a Desmos accident was a single, fixed point that every possible sum line must pass through.  Once you have that point, you can test all four answer choices instantly:

$$x_p = \frac{90 - t}{k}, \qquad y_p = 90n$$

Plug $x_p$ into each candidate expression.  The one that doesn't give $90n$ is impossible.  No casework, no sign‑tracking, no "is it $a$ or $b$?"

The full manuscript follows the discovery from the first mistake to the proof, including the failed attempts and the intermediate machinery that almost worked but didn't.

If you only take one thing from this: every transversal‑angle sum problem has a single pivot point.  Find it once, and the test does the rest.

entries.title: The Exponential Ratio Invariant
entries.body:
I kept seeing the same question: "$f(x)=a\cdot b^{cx}$ … $f(m)$ is $p\%$ greater/less than $f(n)$."  The textbook method is to compute both function values, subtract, divide, and convert.  But the initial value $a$ appears in both numbers and cancels.

That means the percent change depends only on the base, the coefficient, and how far apart the exponents are.  The formula that emerges is:

$$p = 100\,\bigl|\, b^{\,c(m-n)} - 1 \,\bigr|$$

No sign analysis, no "growth versus decay" decision.  The absolute value handles everything, and the word "than" in the question always tells you which exponent is the denominator.

The manuscript walks through the "Than Denominator Rule", the master multiplier $M = b^{c(m-n)}$, and five SAT‑style drills that work forward, backward, with fractional exponents, and with decay — all solved in one line each.

entries.title: A Unified Five-in-One Proof
entries.body:
I noticed something strange: the five angle relationships that parallel lines give us (alternate, corresponding, co‑interior, vertically opposite, adjacent supplementary) all feel like different statements, but under the hood they come from the same algebraic identity.

What if you only had to remember one thing — and the rest are just its reflections?

The idea is that all five reduce to a single invariant equation:

$$\angle_1 + \angle_2 = 180^\circ$$

when you label the diagram correctly and follow the transversal.  The manuscript (still in preparation) will show how the invariant reproduces each theorem without separate memorisation.

If I'm right, this turns a list of five into one.  If I'm wrong, I'll post the messy attempt anyway — that's how most of these shortcuts start.

entries.title: Absolute Value Invariant Explorations
entries.body:
I noticed a pattern in absolute value equations of the form $a|bx+c| = d$. The solution simplifies to $x = -2c/b$, independent of $a$ and $d$. This was unexpected — the coefficients $a$ and $d$ both cancel out.

But that was just the beginning. What if the expression inside the absolute value isn't linear? What if it's quadratic, or trigonometric, or something else entirely? I'm currently exploring whether the invariance generalizes to $|f(x)| = k$, and whether the solution's independence from $k$ depends on symmetry properties of $f$.

The main questions I'm chasing:
- For which functions $f$ does $|f(x)| = k$ have a $k$-independent solution?
- Does the symmetry of $f$ around its zero matter?
- What happens when $f$ has multiple zeros?

I'll post what I find, even the messy attempts.
